covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832.

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

electronAffinity.note: PubChem lists no electron affinity for this element.

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000a.

polarizability.note: Recommended value of the 2018 table: from experiment where it is precise enough, otherwise from high-level calculation.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('4.15×10⁴ milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('4.12×10² milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: average of solar and meteoritic values; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

crystal.reference: Bernstein, B. T.; Smith, J. F. (1959). Acta Crystallographica 12, 419.

molarHeatCapacity.note: At 25 °C and 1 bar, per mole of atoms, for the form stable at 25 °C (CRC Handbook, 95th ed.).

uses.text: Lime (calcium oxide) is used above all in steelmaking, then in chemicals, flue-gas cleaning, construction and water treatment.
Gypsum (calcium sulfate) makes wallboard and plaster and is used in cement and agriculture.
Calcium metal extracts thorium, uranium and zirconium from their compounds and removes oxygen, sulfur and carbon from alloys.

hazardStatements.text: In contact with water releases flammable gas

hazards.note: EU harmonised classification (CLP Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008, Annex VI), via PubChem.

crust.note: Earth's crust, as given (mg/kg is parts per million by mass).

ocean.note: Sea water, mg/L read as mg/kg: a litre of sea water is taken as one kilogram (it is slightly heavier; the difference cannot be seen on a logarithmic scale).

body.note: Grams in the 70 kg reference adult of ICRP Publication 23, divided by its mass.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.092, massive_stars 0.512, white_dwarfs 0.397); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 80 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: '39% of Ca ... come from SNe Ia' (figure reading 0.397). Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

air.text: Oxidises in air to a film that sticks and protects it; calcium burns with a red flame.

water.text: Reacts readily with water, giving calcium hydroxide and hydrogen.

acids.text: Reacts with dilute acids, giving off hydrogen.

splitting.note: Measured by Arbes et al. (1994) with stored ions, as quoted in arXiv:1011.5949 Sec. I and arXiv:physics/0611134. A uncertainty derived as splitting uncertainty / 4. Negative A: inverted structure.

gamma.note: Γ/2π from NIST's A_ki = 2.18e+08 s⁻¹ (accuracy class B+), taking the upper level to decay only on this line; where it has other decay channels the true linewidth is slightly larger.

laserCooling.note: The 1990 paper (same as Sr) trapped 40,42,43,44Ca on this 1S0-1P1 line. First BEC of a true alkaline-earth element (2009); alkaline-earth-like Yb was first, in 2003. Wavelength is NIST's value for the element; the isotope shift for this isotope is not applied. NIST observed value, 3 decimals.

gamma.note: Γ/2π from NIST's A_ki = 1.4e+08 s⁻¹ (accuracy class C), taking the upper level to decay only on this line; where it has other decay channels the true linewidth is slightly larger.

laserCooling.note: Repump 3d 2D3/2 - 4p 2P1/2. first_cooled = the paper the Olmschenk ion catalog lists as first 'trapped/laser cooled'.

siHistory.text: 40Ca (456 THz) is a recommended radiation for realizing the metre.
40Ca+ (411 THz) is a secondary representation of the second.

plantRole.text: Binds the pectins of cell walls, stabilizes membranes, and acts as a messenger inside the cell; it moves only in the xylem, so young tissue shows a shortage first.

humanRole.text: Builds bones and teeth, and signals muscle contraction, nerve transmission and blood clotting.

roles.text: The main mineral of bone and eggshell and a signal in nerves and muscles; dairy cows can get milk fever when their blood calcium drops at calving.
Baker's yeast needs it to grow and uses it as a signal, for example under stress or in response to mating pheromone.
Kept at low levels; some bacteria use it to hold secreted enzymes together, to form spores or in calcium-binding proteins.

history.note: PubChem lists the year as 'Ancient' because lime was used in antiquity. Davy obtained the impure metal, building on Berzelius and Pontin's electrolysis of lime into a mercury amalgam.

prose.text: Calcium is a reactive alkaline-earth metal that we almost never see pure; instead we meet it in bones and teeth, in seashells, chalk, limestone and marble, and in the pectin 'glue' that holds neighbouring plant cells together. Calcium-48, only 0.187 % of natural calcium, is remarkably rich in neutrons yet almost stable, decaying with a half-life of about 2.9 × 10¹⁹ years. The reason is a nuclear shell effect: its 20 protons and 28 neutrons are both 'magic numbers' that close nuclear shells, so it is doubly magic. Beams of calcium-48 were used to create the heaviest elements yet made. The atom itself is [Ar] 4s², ground term ¹S₀.
